# Y8SQ format

> This is an English translation of the [Japanese original](../bytecode.md). Where the two differ, the Japanese version is authoritative.

**This document is the specification of the "Y8SQ format", the byte sequence that represents a sequence.** This is the format that the compiler of Y8960 BASIC Extension produces from MML; this document collects the information needed to write a cross-compiler that turns MML into the same byte sequence on a PC, or a player that plays the Y8SQ format.

**The Y8SQ format also represents sound chips that Y8960 BASIC Extension cannot play.** These are OPL3, OPNA and OPNB (see "Device numbers and channel numbers" below); Y8960 BASIC Extension skips their tracks and plays the rest. This ROM reads the SSGS, OPLLEX, OPL2EX, SCC and OPM parts, and behavior specific to this ROM is written separately as "this ROM's reader".

How to write MML itself is in [`basic-reference.md`](basic-reference.md), the entries of the Y8960 Sequencer BIOS are in [`sequencer-bios.md`](sequencer-bios.md), and the form of the file that carries ADPCM voice files together with their settings is in [`pcmfile.md`](pcmfile.md).

This document specifies two things: **the series of events and its meaning**, and the **form of the block** that contains it and hands it over ("Block" onward). The latter is what `MSAVE` writes out and what `MLOAD` and `SQALLC` read.

**Where a range is given for a value, values outside that range must not be written.** The same applies to limits and to what is stated as an obligation on the writer. How the reader handles what must not be written is not specified, except where stated individually.

## Tracks and sequences

A **track** is the unit of playback; it consists of one byte sequence and the pair of device number and channel number that plays it.

A **sequence** is a group of 16 tracks, which start at the same time and advance together. There are 4 sequences.

- The byte sequence of a track is a **series of events** and ends with `FF`
- One track can play only one channel. Chords are written with multiple tracks
- Which **event table** a track is written in is determined by the track's device and channel
  (see "The two tables" below)

### Device numbers and channel numbers

0-4 are the same numbers that `MASSIGN` takes. **5-7 and 9 are not used** — they are not numbers that must not be written, but numbers to which no chip is assigned, and the reader skips them as "devices it does not play".

| Device number | Sound chip | Channel numbers |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | SSGS | 0-5 |
| 1 | OPLLEX | 0-8, 10 is rhythm |
| 2 | OPL2EX | 0-8, 9 is ADPCM, 10 is rhythm |
| 3 | SCC | 0-4 |
| 4 | OPM | 0-7 are FM |
| 5-7 | (not assigned) | |
| 8 | OPL3 | 0-17 are FM (2OP), 18-23 are FM (4OP), 24 is rhythm |
| 9 | (not assigned) | |
| 10 | OPNA | 0-5 are FM, 6-8 are SSG, 9 is rhythm, 10 is ADPCM-B |
| 11 | OPNB | 0-5 are FM, 6-8 are SSG, 9 is ADPCM-A, 10 is ADPCM-B |

**OPNB is not distinguished from OPNB-B.** It is OPNB-B that has 6 FM channels; OPNB lacks FM channels 0 and 3. Making sure that a sequence played on OPNB does not use those two is the responsibility of whoever creates the sequence; the block does not say which chip it is for.

**OPL3's 2OP channels 0-8 are in the chip's first register set, and 9-17 in the second.** A 4OP channel is a pair of two 2OP channels.

| 4OP | Paired 2OP |
|---|---|
| 18 | 0 and 3 |
| 19 | 1 and 4 |
| 20 | 2 and 5 |
| 21 | 9 and 12 |
| 22 | 10 and 13 |
| 23 | 11 and 14 |

- **Whether a pair is used is decided by the track assignment.** In a block that has a track on a 4OP channel, that pair belongs to that track. There is no event that represents switching to 4OP, and it is not switched by register writes (`E0` `E8`) either — how to configure the chip is the reader's job
- **Whether a pair is played as 4OP or as two 2OP channels is decided by the selected voice.** When it is two 2OP channels, key-on and pitch are written to the two channels at the same time
- Voices go into the same set as OPLLEX and OPL2EX (see "OPLLEX, OPL2EX and OPL3 voices" below)

**Exclusive channels.** A single block cannot have tracks on both members of the following pairs.

| Device | Exclusive pair |
|---|---|
| OPLLEX, OPL2EX | Channel 10 (rhythm) and 6-8 |
| OPL3 | Channel 24 (rhythm) and 6-8 |
| OPL3 | A 4OP channel and the two 2OP channels it pairs |

A block that has a track on the rhythm channel enters rhythm mode when the sequence starts playing from the beginning, and a block that has tracks on channels 6-8 leaves rhythm mode. A block that has neither leaves the mode as it is. OPL3's rhythm is the same as the OPLLEX and OPL2EX rhythm, except that its channel number is 24.

**OPNB's ADPCM-A (channel 9) is treated the same as a rhythm channel.** One track strikes the six ADPCM-A channels as instruments (see "Rhythm channels" below).

## Time

The **tick** is the unit of time, and **a quarter note is 48 ticks**. Because this is divisible by 3, triplets come out as whole numbers, and a 64th note is also a whole number, at 3 ticks.

**The tempo determines the length of one tick, not the number of ticks.** A quarter note is 48 ticks at every tempo; a tempo event changes only how many seconds one tick lasts. Therefore changing the tempo does not change the ratios between note lengths.

An event that has a length **waits** for that length before proceeding to the next event.

## Pitch

**Pitch is in equal temperament, with A in O4 (note number 57) at 440 Hz.** If the block has a master pitch in its meta information, A4 is set to that frequency (see "Meta information" below).

## Event layout

**The upper bits of the opcode determine how many bytes follow.**

| Opcode | What follows |
|---|---|
| `00`-`3F` | Length (1-2 bytes, see below) |
| `40`-`7F` | Nothing |
| `80`-`BF` | 1 byte |
| `C0`-`CF` | 1 byte, then a length |
| `D0`-`DF` | 2 bytes |
| `E0`-`EF` | 3 bytes |
| `F0`-`FE` | 4 bytes |
| `FF` | End of track |

**The purpose of this rule is to allow unknown opcodes to be skipped.** Even without knowing the meaning, the size is known, so the reader can proceed to the start of the next event. That is why **opcodes are arranged by form, not by meaning.**

### Encoding of lengths

| | |
|---|---|
| 0-127 ticks | 1 byte. The value as is |
| 128 ticks or more | 2 bytes. The first byte is `80h` + the high byte, the second byte is the low byte |

**Bit7 of the first byte marks the long form.** Most notes are shorter than 128 ticks, so the ordinary case takes one byte. **Values up to 8191 ticks may be written** (the first byte of the long form is `80`-`9F`). The largest that can be produced from MML is a double-dotted whole note, 336 ticks.

### The two tables

**The FM family and the PSG family have separate event tables.** Which one a track is written in is determined by the track's device and channel, so the byte sequence itself carries no mark.

| Table | Tracks |
|---|---|
| FM family | All channels of OPLLEX, OPL2EX, OPM and OPL3. The channels of OPNA and OPNB other than SSG (FM, rhythm, ADPCM-A, ADPCM-B) |
| PSG family | All channels of SSGS and SCC. The SSG of OPNA and OPNB |

Rhythm channels (the rhythm of OPLLEX, OPL2EX, OPL3 and OPNA, and OPNB's ADPCM-A) and ADPCM channels (OPL2EX's ADPCM, and the ADPCM-B of OPNA and OPNB) are written with the FM family table.

**Device numbers with no sound chip assigned belong to neither table.** The reader skips such tracks ("Device numbers and channel numbers"), so it never reads their events. Which table they are written in is decided when a chip is assigned to that number.

**In each group, the lower half is common to both families and the upper half is per family.**

| Group | Common | FM family | PSG family |
|---|---|---|---|
| Followed by a length | `00`-`1F` | `20`-`2F` | `30`-`3F` |
| Followed by nothing | `40`-`5F` | `60`-`6F` | `70`-`7F` |
| 1 byte | `80`-`9F` | `A0`-`AF` | `B0`-`BF` |
| 1 byte + length | `C0`-`C7` | `C8`-`CF` | — |
| 2 bytes | `D0`-`D7` | `D8`-`DB` | `DC`-`DF` |
| 3 bytes | `E0`-`EF` | — | — |
| 4 bytes | `F0`-`FE` | — | — |

**The same operation uses the same opcode.** Selecting a voice is `82`, and whether that is an FM voice or an SCC waveform is decided by the driver. Notes are also common; whether the pitch becomes an F-Number or a divider value is the driver's job.

## Running state

A track holds the following values while playing. **Events rewrite them, and notes read them.**

| Value | Initial value | Events that change it |
|---|---|---|
| Octave | 4 | `40` `41` `80` |
| Volume (0-127, 1 is 0.75 dB) | 99 (MML `V8`) | `81` |
| Voice number | 0 | `82` `85` |
| Quantize (1-8) | 8 | `83` |
| Software envelope (PSG family) | 0 (none) | `B2` |
| Whether SCC volume is corrected by the table (PSG family) | 1 (corrected) | `B3` |
| SSGS channel volume (0-128, linear) | 128 | `B4` |
| Pitch offsets of subchannels 1-3 in effect mode (channel 2 of OPNA and OPNB) | 0 for all three | `E9` |

**A note carries only the semitone; the octave is running state.** The note opcodes `00`-`0B` are the 12 semitones from c to b, and the actual pitch is octave × 12 + semitone. `0F` and `10` correspond to semitones −1 and 12, and step into the adjacent octave for that one note only (the octave is not changed).

**Volume is 0-127, and 1 corresponds to 0.75 dB.** 127 is the voice as it is (the loudest), and each step down from 127 makes it 0.75 dB quieter. MML `V`*n* is 0-15 and maps to 4*n* + 67 (`V15` is 127, `V0` is 67; one step is 3 dB). `@V`*n* takes 0-127 as is (on SSGS tracks it becomes `B4` instead of `81`; see below).

- The reader rounds to the chip's step, and any reduction beyond the range the chip has stops at the bottom of that range. On FM sound chips, it is added to the attenuation of the operators that reach the output under the algorithm
- **On those that have only a 4-bit volume** (OPLLEX FM, SSGS, SCC, the SSG of OPNA and OPNB), the volume is lowered by (127 − volume) divided by 4 (fraction truncated) steps, and not lowered below 15 steps. `V`*n* comes out exactly 15−*n* steps below the top. `@V` values finer than `V` sound as this calculation gives
- **On those that hold volume as a linear gain** (the ADPCM level), the 0.75 dB steps are converted to gain
- **`81` on SSGS acts on the SSG's own 4-bit amplitude.** The per-channel linear volume registers (`20h`-`22h` `24h`-`26h`) are set by `B4`, not `81`, and the volume from outside the sequence is not applied to them either

**Quantize expresses the fraction of the length during which a note sounds, in eighths.** 8 is the full length, in which case the key-off is left to the next key-on. A short note for which the division comes out as 0 is rounded up to 1 tick — it does not become a note without a key-off.

**A note immediately followed by `45` (tie/legato) or `D2 8000h` (portamento from the sounding pitch) sounds for its full length regardless of quantize.** Only the one event immediately after the note is examined; if another event comes in between, quantize applies. The gate of the last note in a chain is derived from **that note's own length** — not from the total of the
joined lengths.

**0 does not exist as a value.** MML `Qn` is 1-8, and `MTRK` rejects `Q0`. `83 00` must not be written.

**Notes before an event that selects a voice play with the initial voice.** The initial number is 0, which means the same as writing `82 00` (what it refers to is in the `82` table below). It returns to this value at the start of each pass.

**However, on FM sound chip channels and on SCC, the writer issues an event that selects a voice before the first key-on.** This applies to the FM channels of OPLLEX, OPL2EX, OPL3, OPM, OPNA and OPNB, and to SCC. For voices represented by records (`85` below), the reader has no table in which to look up the contents by number, so the writer issues `85` and puts the record in the block. OPLLEX's built-in voices are selected with `82`. The initial value may be relied on only for channels where the `82` number alone is enough — SSGS, the SSG of OPNA and OPNB, and the ADPCM channels.

**The software envelope also returns to 0 (none) at the start of each pass.** If the argument of `B2` is 1 or more, the block must contain the envelope record with that number (chunk `04`) — the reader has no table in which to look up the contents by number, so, as with `85`, this is **an obligation on the writer.** The record holds the speeds directly (see "Chunk `04`" below). The rest of the behavior (attack, decay, sustain, release, the relation to `V`, and not returning to the attack on ties and legato) is specified by the "Software envelope — `@E`*n*" section of [`basic-reference.md`](basic-reference.md).

**The tempo belongs to the sequence, not to the track.** Whichever track writes a tempo event, the tick length of the whole sequence changes. **The initial value is 120** (quarter notes per minute), and like a track's running state, **it returns to this value at the start of each pass** — the last `84` of the previous pass is not carried over to the next pass.

## Event table

### Common

| Opcode | Followed by | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `00`-`0B` | Length | Note. c c+ d d+ e f f+ g g+ a a+ b |
| `0C` | Length | Rest. Stops the sounding note and waits |
| `0E` | Length | Wait only. Does not touch the key |
| `0F` | Length | Note. b of the octave below (MML `c-`). Does not change the octave |
| `10` | Length | Note. c of the octave above (MML `b+`). Does not change the octave |
| `40` | — | Raise the octave by one |
| `41` | — | Lower the octave by one |
| `42` | — | Loop start |
| `43` | — | Da capo |
| `44` | — | Coda. A marker that does nothing during playback |
| `45` | — | Tie/legato. A property of the **next note**; takes no time itself |
| `80` | 1 | Octave (0-9) |
| `81` | 1 | Volume (0-127) |
| `82` | 1 | Voice number (see below) |
| `83` | 1 | Quantize (1-8). **0 must not be written** (see below) |
| `84` | 1 | Tempo (quarter notes per minute, 32 or more) |
| `85` | 1 | Which of the voices held by this sequence (0-31; see below) |
| `86` | 1 | Segno. Number (0-3). A marker that does nothing during playback |
| `87` | 1 | Panpot (0-255; see below) |
| `C0` | 1+length | Note number. Specifies the pitch without changing the octave. MML `N`*n* is *n* + 12 (`N` counts from O1 C, note numbers count from O0 C) |
| `D0` | 2 | Pitch bend. Cents, signed. Takes effect immediately, even on a sounding note |
| `D1` | 2 | Relative pitch bend. Cents, signed, added to the current value |
| `D2` | 2 | Portamento. Cents, signed. `8000h` means "from the currently sounding pitch" |
| `D3` | 2 | End of block. The following 2 bytes are the **distance to the end of the group** |
| `D4` | 2 | Fine. Arrival counter number (0-7), arrival count at which it fires (1-255) |
| `D5` | 2 | Dal segno. **Distance to the segno** (ignored if 0) |
| `E0` | 3 | Register write. Register number, data, mask (see below) |
| `E1` | 3 | Start of block. Iteration on which it is played, **distance to the next block** (0 if last) |
| `E2` | 3 | Loop end. Repeat count (0 is infinite), **distance to the loop start** |
| `E8` | 3 | Register write to the second port. Same form as `E0` (see below) |
| `E9` | 3 | Pitch of a subchannel in effect mode. Subchannel number (1-3), offset from the parent (signed 16-bit, in units of 1/64 semitone) (see "OPM and OPN-family voices" below) |
| `F0` | 4 | To coda. Arrival counter number (0-7), arrival count at which it fires (1-255), **distance to the coda** (ignored if 0) |
| `FF` | — | End of track |

**There are two opcodes that select a voice, and which one is used is determined by the number.** MML `@n` maps to one of them.

| Opcode | Argument | |
|---|---|---|
| `82` | 1 | **A number the chip resolves itself.** What it refers to depends on the device (table below) |
| `85` | 1 | **Which of the voices held by this sequence (0-31).** All voices and waveforms represented by records use this |

What `82` refers to.

**On devices whose chip has no built-in voices, `82` refers to nothing.** All voices are represented by records and are issued with `85`. MML `@65`-`@127` written to OPL2EX FM becomes `82` (`@`*n* − 64) and sounds as [`basic-reference.md`](basic-reference.md) says: "ignored (the previous voice remains)".

| Device | |
|---|---|
| OPLLEX | The chip's built-in presets. **Bit5-4 are the bank and bit3-0 are the preset within the bank**; bit7-6 are ignored. Preset 0 is the chip's user voice, and what sounds is not guaranteed (it is whatever voice is loaded at the time). MML `@65`-`@127` becomes `@`*n* − 64. The voices of the MML voice table (`@0`-`@63`) are separate from these and are issued with `85` |
| OPL2EX ADPCM channel | Voice file number (0-63). Not a record, so it does not go into the set |
| SSGS | Mixer and envelope settings. All bits are meaningful |
| SSG of OPNA and OPNB | Same as SSGS |
| ADPCM-B of OPNA and OPNB | Voice file number (0-63). Same as the OPL2EX ADPCM channel |
| OPL2EX FM, SCC, OPL3, OPM, FM of OPNA and OPNB | **Refers to nothing.** This is because the chip has no built-in voices. **The reader ignores it regardless of the argument** |

**Voices that have records are held by the sequence itself.** For the voices of the OPLLEX and OPL2EX voice tables (`0`-`63`) and voices created by programs (`128`-`191`), and for SCC's preset waveforms and waveforms created by programs, the records are copied into the sequence's voice set at compile time, and from then on `85` refers to an index into the set. **Everything playback needs is closed within the sequence**, so handing over a single block is enough, without preparing voices separately.

- The set holds up to **32** per sequence. Writing the same `@n` any number of times takes only one
- The contents of the set are written out as chunks `01` `02` of the block (see below)
- **OPL3 also uses this set.** 2OP voices are written out as chunk `01`, and 4OP voices as chunk `42`
- **OPM, OPNA and OPNB each have their own set per device, separate from this set.**
  Each holds up to 32 (indexes 0-31), and `85` on that device's tracks
  refers to that device's set. The contents are written out as chunk `40`
  (see "OPM and OPN-family voices" below). The set of OPLLEX, OPL2EX, SCC and OPL3 and
  the sets of OPM, OPNA and OPNB are each distinct, even for the same index
- **A track on which notes were written in MML without selecting a voice also puts the record of the `@0` voice
  into the set and names it with `85`** (the obligation on the writer in "Running state" above). Otherwise the block could say only "voice 0", and the reader has no table to look it up in
- OPLLEX loads a voice into the chip's user voice registers at the moment it is selected, so **one block can hold only one at a time** (a limitation of the chip)

**The mask of a register write (`E0`) has 1 in the bits to keep.** The register becomes `(current value AND mask) OR data`. A mask of 0 makes the whole register the data. The register number is the chip's own on every sound chip; the ranges accepted on the sound chips this ROM plays are in [`basic-reference.md`](basic-reference.md).

**`E8` writes to the second set of registers on chips that have two sets.** These are the registers of OPL3, OPNA and OPNB whose addresses start at `100h` (the side where address pin A1 is 1); the register number holds the low 8 bits. The form and the meaning of the mask are the same as `E0`. The reader for a device without a second set ignores it.

**Settings of which there is only one set for the whole chip are not managed by the sequence.** However, rhythm mode and OPL3's 4OP are decided by the track assignment as in "Exclusive channels" above, and the overall volume of rhythm and ADPCM-A can be written with `AB` (see "Rhythm channels" below). **OPM's noise on/off and the effect mode of OPNA and OPNB are not among these settings** — the register belongs to the whole chip, but it affects only one channel, so the voice holds it as that channel's property (see "OPM and OPN-family voices" below). The LFO, OPM's noise frequency and the like are what is not managed, and no track holds them. Of these, the noise frequency also affects only one channel, but the sequence does not manage it. They can be written with `E0` `E8`, but making sure that tracks playing the same chip do not conflict is the responsibility of whoever creates the sequence. Initialization before playback starts is also done outside the sequence.

**The value of the panpot (`87`) is the value of the Y8960 panning register as is**: 1 is far left, 128 is center, and 255 is far right. **The meaning of 0 is not specified** — it is a value the Y8960 specification does not define, and this ROM's reader writes it to the register as is. On chips that can only switch the left and right outputs on or off, the value is rounded as follows.

| Value | SSGS, OPLLEX, OPL2EX, SCC | OPL3, OPM, OPNA, OPNB |
|---|---|---|
| 1-64 | As the value | Left only |
| 65-191 | As the value | Both |
| 192-255 | As the value | Right only |

- **OPL3 treats output A as left and B as right.** Outputs C and D are not touched — the reader leaves their current values. The initial values of C and D are decided by initialization outside the sequence
- **On OPL3's 4OP channels, it is written to both channels of the pair.** This is the same whether the pair is played as 4OP or as two 2OP channels
- It takes effect on SSGS, OPLLEX FM and rhythm, OPL2EX FM, rhythm and ADPCM, SCC, OPL3 FM and rhythm, and OPM and the FM, rhythm, ADPCM-A and ADPCM-B of OPNA and OPNB.
  Readers for other devices and channels ignore it
- **On rhythm channels and ADPCM-A, all instruments get the same panning.**
  To vary it per instrument, use register writes. OPLLEX and OPL2EX rhythm sounds play with the panning of channels 6-8, so the reader writes the same value to those three (OPLLEX `50h`+6 to +8, OPL2EX `F6h`+6 to +8). For the OPL2EX ADPCM channel, `FFh`
- It is not running state, and does not return at the start of a pass. **The panning before playback starts is decided by initialization outside the sequence** (for SSGS, OPLLEX, OPL2EX and SCC, this ROM's `CALL MINIT` sets it to center). For a piece that relies on panning, the writer issues `87` at the start of the track
- MML `i`*n* becomes `87`

**Segno (`86`) and coda (`44`) are markers that do nothing during playback.** The jump targets are held as distances by dal segno (`D5`) and to coda (`F0`), so the reader just skips the markers. The markers exist for the writer's convenience: when a piece is written in several parts, a part written later can find jump targets within the parts written earlier.

### FM family only

| Opcode | Followed by | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `A8` | 1 | Rhythm channel. Which of the instruments struck next get an accent (bitmap) |
| `A9` | 1 | Rhythm channel. Normal volume of all instruments (0-15, 0-31 on OPNA and OPNB) |
| `AA` | 1 | Rhythm channel. Accent volume (0-15, 0-31 on OPNA and OPNB). Common to all instruments |
| `AB` | 1 | Rhythm channel. Overall volume (0-63). OPNA rhythm and OPNB ADPCM-A only (see below) |
| `C8` | 1+length | Rhythm channel. Instruments to strike (bitmap), and the length to wait afterwards |
| `D8` | 2 | Rhythm channel. Instruments (bitmap), and the normal volume of those instruments (0-15, 0-31 on OPNA and OPNB) |
| `D9` | 2 | ADPCM-A. Instruments (bitmap), and the number of the sample those instruments play (0-255) |

### Rhythm channels

**A rhythm channel is a channel that strikes a set of instruments.** The set to strike, accents and volumes are all named with an instrument bitmap. The bit order of the bitmap is **exactly the order of the chip's registers**, and differs by device (see below). Which bit an MML instrument letter maps to is decided by the writer (the MML compiler).

| Device and channel | Instruments | Bits used |
|---|---|---|
| Channel 10 of OPLLEX and OPL2EX, channel 24 of OPL3 | 5 rhythm sounds | bit4-0 |
| Channel 9 of OPNA | 6 rhythm sounds | bit5-0 |
| Channel 9 of OPNB | 6 ADPCM-A channels | bit5-0 |

Unused bits are ignored.

**Normal volume is held per instrument.** `D8` sets the normal volume of the instruments whose bits are set in the first byte to the value of the second byte, and does not touch the other instruments. `A9` *n* is the same as `D8` with all used bits set. MML `@B`*n* `@S`*n* `@M`*n* `@C`*n* `@H`*n* become `D8` with only one instrument's bit set, and `V`*n* and `@V`*n* become `A9`.

**Per-instrument volume values are 0-15 on OPLLEX, OPL2EX and OPL3, and 0-31 on OPNA and OPNB.** Each is exactly the range of the per-instrument volume that the chip has, and larger is louder.

**The overall volume (`AB`) is the single volume that the chip has for OPNA's rhythm and OPNB's ADPCM-A, and 0-63 is written to the chip as is.** Larger is louder. It is not running state, and does not return at the start of a pass. The value before playback starts is decided by initialization outside the sequence. Readers other than for channel 9 of OPNA and OPNB ignore it.

**Rhythm volumes (`A9` `AA` `D8`) are not running state.** They do not return at the start of a pass; when the sequence starts playing from the beginning and the block enters rhythm mode (on OPNA and OPNB, when playback starts), the normal volume becomes 8 for all instruments and the accent volume becomes 15 (24 and 31 on OPNA and OPNB).

**ADPCM-A instruments play the sample bound to them with `D9`.** `D9` binds the sample with the number in the second byte to the ADPCM-A channels whose bits are set in the first byte. Where the samples are placed is held by chunk `41` (see below).

- The binding is not running state either, and does not return at the start of a pass. When playback starts,
  no instrument is bound to anything. **The writer issues
  `D9` at the start of the track for every instrument it strikes**
- **The writer puts the chunk `41` with each number that `D9` names into the block**
- Readers other than for channel 9 of OPNB ignore `D9`

**The value of `A8` applies to all subsequent strikes until the next `A8`.** Therefore the writer always issues `A8` after any position that playback can reach from elsewhere, before the first strike. Otherwise the accent of an earlier strike remains, depending on the path taken. Those positions are as follows.

- The start of the track (when `MTRK` is written in parts, the start of each part too)
- After a loop start (`42`) and after a loop end (`E2`)
- A block start (`E1`), and the end of a block group
- Segno (`86`) and coda (`44`)

Elsewhere, `A8` may be omitted if the accent is the same as for the immediately preceding strike.

The instrument bits of OPLLEX, OPL2EX and OPL3 are in the same order as the rhythm registers of the three chips.

| Bit | Instrument |
|---|---|
| bit4 | Bass drum |
| bit3 | Snare drum |
| bit2 | Tom |
| bit1 | Top cymbal |
| bit0 | Hi-hat |

OPNA instruments are in the same order as the chip's rhythm key-on register, and OPNB instruments in the same order as the ADPCM-A key-on register.

### PSG family only

| Opcode | Followed by | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `B0` | 1 | Hardware envelope shape of SSGS and of the SSG of OPNA and OPNB. Readers for other devices ignore it |
| `B2` | 1 | **Software envelope number** (0-31). 0 is none. Takes effect on SSGS, SCC and the SSG of OPNA and OPNB; readers for other devices ignore it |
| `B3` | 1 | **Whether SCC volume is corrected by the table.** 0 does not correct and 1 corrects (see below). Takes effect only on SCC; readers for other devices ignore it |
| `B4` | 1 | **SSGS channel volume** (0-128, linear; see below). Takes effect only on SSGS; readers for other devices ignore it |
| `DC` | 2 | Hardware envelope period (16-bit) of SSGS and of the SSG of OPNA and OPNB. Readers for other devices ignore it |

**What `B3` selects is whether the volume (converted to 0-15) passes through a table before it is written to the SCC volume register.** 1 passes it through the table, and 0 writes it as is. The table and its meaning are specified by "SCC volume" in [`basic-reference.md`](basic-reference.md). Like the volume event (`81`), it takes effect immediately even on a sounding note, and it also applies to software envelope values. **It returns to 1 at the start of each pass.** The argument is 0 or 1, and other values must not be written.

**`B4` writes the value as is to the SSGS channel's linear volume register (`20h`-`22h` `24h`-`26h`).** 128 passes the sound through unchanged, 0 is silence, and values in between are proportional to amplitude. It is separate from the 4-bit amplitude set by `81`, and the actual volume is the product of the two. Volume from outside the sequence (this ROM's `VOLUME`, fades, mute) applies only to the `81` side and not to `B4`. It takes effect immediately even on a sounding note. **It returns to 128 at the start of each pass.** MML `@V`*n* on SSGS becomes `B4`, and `V`*n* stays `81`. Values of 129 or more must not be written.

## Writing jump targets

**Loops and jumps hold a signed 16-bit distance, neither an address nor a position within the track.** The track's byte sequence is placed at a different location each time it is loaded, so jump targets that name a location cannot be used.

**The distance is counted from the position after the two bytes of the distance have been read.** The reader just adds the distance at the point where it finished reading the event. Going backwards uses a negative number (two's complement).

### Repeats

The reader keeps the **current iteration count** for each level of loop nesting. **Nesting is up to 4 levels.**

- At a loop start (`42`), the reader pushes one level with the iteration count set to 1
- At a loop end (`E2`), if the iteration count has reached the repeat count, the reader pops one level and proceeds; if not, it increments the iteration count by 1 and returns to the start
- A repeat count of 0 is infinite. The iteration count stops at 255

### Blocks (first and second endings)

**A block is a section that is played only on a given iteration.** Consecutive blocks form one **group**.

- At the start of a block (`E1`), the block's iteration is compared with the current iteration count. If they are equal, playback proceeds into the block; if not, it advances by the "distance to the next block"
- **A block whose "distance to the next block" is 0 is the last of the group**, and playback proceeds into it even if the iteration count does not match. This is what is played when no block matches
- The end of a block (`D3`) jumps unconditionally to the end of the group

### Segno, coda and fine

**To coda (`F0`) and fine (`D4`) fire by arrival count.** The reader keeps **8 arrival counters** per track, and each event holds the number of one of them.

- Each time the event is reached, the counter is incremented by 1, and if it equals the arrival count for firing, the event fires
- **The counter is not reset when the event fires.** It keeps counting, so the same to coda is not taken twice on the next pass
- The counter returns to 0 only when the sequence is started **anew**. When repeating for another pass, it is carried over. **This is what makes pieces that go from da capo to the coda work** — the pass that ended at da capo is the first arrival at the to coda, and the second arrival, on the next pass, jumps
- **The counter is one byte and wraps around every 256.** After 255 it returns to 0 and keeps counting, so **the same to coda fires again every 256 arrivals.** This count is reached only when a piece that never ends keeps playing; until then, the rules above apply
- **The arrival count for firing is 1-255.** 0 must not be written

**Da capo (`43`) and fine (`D4`) end the pass of the whole sequence, not just of that track.** Whatever the other tracks still hold is not played. What happens after that is decided by the repeat count specified when playback was started.

**When a pass ends, whatever is sounding at that point does not stop there.** The next pass starts on the same tick, and what cuts each track's key is the first event of that pass — a note keys off before writing its own pitch, and a rest (`0C`) also keys off before waiting. So a track that starts with a note or a rest loses the previous sound within the same tick.
**`0E` (wait only) does not touch the key, so a track whose next pass starts with `0E` enters the pass keeping the last sound of the previous pass.** The exception is when the passes have used up the repeats and playback ends; there, all tracks are keyed off.

**A jump discards the loop nesting.** After a dal segno or to coda jumps, all stacked iteration counts are popped. A loop entered again at the jump target counts from the first iteration.

## Limits

| | |
|---|---|
| Length of one event | 8191 ticks |
| Length denominator (MML) | 96 (the denominator of `Ln` and of lengths attached directly to notes) |
| Note number (`C0`) | 12-139 (MML `N0`-`N127`) |
| Cents (`D0` `D1` `D2`) | ±1200 |
| Loop nesting | 4 levels |
| Segno numbers | 0-3 |
| Arrival counters per track | 8 |
| Events that take no time, read in a row within one tick | 256 |

**When 256 events that take no time occur in a row, the reader ends that track.** An infinite loop whose contents take no time, or a dal segno that goes back to a point before itself, would, if not stopped, keep running inside the interrupt and make the machine unresponsive. **These cannot be rejected at the time of writing**, so this ROM cuts off at 256 and ends the track — if the piece is wrong anyway, it is better for it to sound wrong. The count is incremented for each event read, and starts over when an event that takes time is encountered.

## Block

**A block is the form that carries one whole sequence as a unit.** `MSAVE` writes it, and `MLOAD` and `SQALLC` read it. It consists of one header followed by a series of **chunks**. There is no end marker; **the length in the header determines where it ends.**

### Header (7 bytes)

| Offset | Size | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 4 | `59 38 53 51` (`"Y8SQ"`) |
| 4 | 1 | Version. Currently `01` |
| 5 | 2 | Byte count of the whole block, including the header. Low byte first |

**All 2-byte numbers are low byte first.**

### Chunks

| Offset | Size | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1 | Type |
| 1 | 2 | Byte count of the contents. Does not include these 3 bytes |
| 3 | n | Contents |

| Type | Contents |
|---|---|
| `00` | **Track.** Track number (0-15), device number, channel number, then the event stream. The event stream ends with `FF`, and that `FF` is included in the length |
| `01` | **OPLLEX and OPL2EX voices, and OPL3 2OP voices.** Index in the voice set (0-31), then a 12-byte record (see "OPLLEX, OPL2EX and OPL3 voices" below). Indexes 32-34 are the OPL2EX and OPL3 rhythm voices (below) |
| `02` | **SCC waveform.** Index in the voice set (0-31), then a 32-byte waveform. The meaning of the index and where it goes are the same as for `01` |
| `03` | **ADPCM voice file.** Voice file number, 1 byte; first block in sample memory, 2 bytes; number of blocks, 2 bytes; sampling frequency (Hz), 2 bytes. A block is a unit of 256 bytes |
| `04` | **Software envelope.** Envelope number (1-31), 1 byte, then AR, DR, SL and RR, 1 byte each (below) |
| `40` | **OPM, OPNA and OPNB FM voices.** Device number, index in the voice set (0-31), then a 32-byte record (see "OPM and OPN-family voices" below) |
| `41` | **ADPCM-A sample.** Device number (11), sample number (0-255), first block in sample memory, 2 bytes; number of blocks, 2 bytes. A block is a unit of 256 bytes |
| `42` | **OPL3 4OP voice.** Device number (8), index in the voice set (0-31), then a 24-byte record (see "OPLLEX, OPL2EX and OPL3 voices" below). The index belongs to the same set as `01` and `02` |
| `80` | **Meta information.** A series of items (see "Meta information" below). The reader need not use it |
| `81`-`FF` | May be skipped. **Even for an unknown type, advancing by the length reaches the next chunk** |

**Types `40`-`7F` are chunks that belong to one device.** The first byte of the contents is the number of the device it belongs to.

**Every track that has a channel is written out.** Tracks with empty contents are written out too — the device/channel pair is part of the block, so the assignment is saved and restored even for a part in which nothing has been written yet.

**Track numbers that are not written get no assignment.** The loading side touches only the tracks that the block names.

### Versions and unknown contents

- **A block whose version is newer than the reader's is not read.** A newer writer may have changed the layout of the header itself, and the length would then have to be read from a different place
- **Types `80` and above may be skipped.** Anything without which playback still works when the reader does not use it goes here
- **Anything for a device the reader does not play may be skipped.** For a track (`00`),
  tell by the device number; for types `40`-`7F`, by the device number at the start of the contents.
  Tracks for devices that are not played are not assigned, and the remaining tracks are played
- **If the reader meets something unknown concerning a device it plays, it does not read the block at all.**
  This covers unknown types `00`-`3F`, and unknown types `40`-`7F` that belong to a device
  it plays. Skipping a voice or waveform while reading would change what sounds

**This ROM's reader plays devices 0-4.** It skips tracks whose device number is 5 or above, and chunks of types `40`-`7F` whose first content byte is a device number of 5 or above. The same applies to the unassigned 5-7 and 9, and to numbers 12 and above, which this format has not yet named. It loads chunk `40` for device 4 into the OPM set. It rejects the whole block for a chunk of types `40`-`7F` that names devices 0-3, for one that names device 4 and is not `40`, and for one whose contents are empty and so have no device number. Skipped tracks are lost when the sequence is written out again with `MSAVE`.

**ADPCM samples are not included in the block.** On an ADPCM channel (the OPL2EX ADPCM, and the OPNA and OPNB ADPCM-B), `@n` is a voice file number issued as `82`, and the actual data is in the sound chip's sample memory. On the OPNB that is ROM.
**Preparing a voice file with the same number at the same place is the job of whoever has the block played.** As a clue for that, chunk `03` holds the location and frequency of each voice file. Its 7 bytes of contents have the same layout as one settings entry of the file that carries samples and settings ([`pcmfile.md`](pcmfile.md)).

- What is written out is the voice files used by tracks on ADPCM channels — those named by `82`, and the initial value 0 if there is a note before the first `82`
- Of those, only the ones placed in sample memory at the time of writing. Ones placed in main RAM or VRAM, and ones that do not yet have a location, are not written, because they would not sound as they are
- The loading side need not use this chunk. This ROM's reader skips it and does not touch sample memory
- **This ROM does not check the contents at all.** It only advances by the declared length; it does not check that the length is 7, nor the voice file number or the block range. Unlike `01` and `02`, the block is not rejected even if the values are corrupt — it is rejected only when the length is corrupt and the following chunks no longer line up with the end of the block
- A reader that **uses** the values must check them itself. The ranges are the same as for one settings entry in [`pcmfile.md`](pcmfile.md)
- **Voice file numbers do not distinguish devices.** If ADPCM
  channels of different devices name the same number, only one chunk `03` can be written, so
  on either chip it points to the same location and frequency

**ADPCM-A samples are not included in the block either.** There is one chunk `41` per sample number named by `D9`, and it holds only the location. ADPCM-A has a fixed playback rate, so it holds no frequency. The order of the chunks has no meaning; if the same number is written twice, the later one remains. If the contents are not 6 bytes, the whole block is rejected. The device number is 11; other numbers and a block count of 0 must not be written.

**The OPL2EX and OPL3 rhythm voices become chunks `01` with indexes 32-34.** Rhythm mode loads three voices into ch6-8 (in order: bass drum, hi-hat and snare drum, tom and top cymbal). No event names them, so they are placed at indexes outside the voice set. They are written out for a sequence that has a track on channel 10 of the OPL2EX, or on channel 24 of the OPL3. A block can hold one set of rhythm voices, and those chips share it.
The loading side need not use them. This ROM loads its own voices when it enters rhythm mode, and skips the ones in the block.

**Indexes 0-31 are the argument of `85` itself.** The order of the chunks has no meaning; if the same index is written twice, the later one remains. A chunk whose index is 35 or above, or whose record length is wrong (12 bytes for `01`, 32 bytes for `02`), causes the whole block to be rejected.

**`01`, `02` and `42` go into the same set.** The index of `42` is also 0-31; one whose index is 32 or above, or whose record is not 24 bytes, causes the whole block to be rejected. The device number is 8; other numbers must not be written. A reader that does not play the OPL3 may skip `42` (only OPL3 tracks name it). The record length is determined by the type, and how the record is read is determined by **the device of the track that names it**. The writing side writes voices as `01` and waveforms as `02`. Even in a block that was loaded and then written out again, the type stays as it was when loaded.

**To check without relying on the type, look at the device of the track that has an `85` naming that index.** For SCC it is a waveform, for an OPL3 4OP channel a 4OP voice, and otherwise an FM voice (2OP). The playing side uses only this.

**On the OPL3, an `85` naming an index whose type does not fit the channel is silently ignored.** This is the case when a 4OP channel names an index of `01`, or a 2OP channel names an index of `42`; the voice stays as it was. The block is not rejected.

**There is one chunk `04` per number that a PSG-family track names with `B2`.**
Only the numbers that are named are written out; 0 is not written. The order of the chunks has no meaning; if the same number is written twice, the later one remains. **A chunk whose number is 0 or 32 and above, or whose contents are not 5 bytes, causes the whole block to be rejected.**

| Value | Contents |
|---|---|
| AR, DR, RR | bit7-4 is the frame count (1-15), bit3-0 the step (1-15). Every that many frames, the value moves by the step. One frame is 1/60 second |
| SL | 0-15 |

The AR, DR and RR values 0-32 taken by `CALL ENV COPY` in [`basic-reference.md`](basic-reference.md) are numbers given to 33 combinations of this form; the "Frames" and "Change" columns of the table in the "Software envelope — `@E`*n*" section are the upper and lower 4 bits respectively. `MSAVE` writes out the values looked up in that table.

### Meta information

**Chunk `80` holds information that playback does not need, and settings without which playback still works.** At most one per block. The reader need only use the items it finds useful, and may skip the whole chunk.

The contents are a series of items; one item has the following form.

| Offset | Size | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1 | Item number |
| 1 | 1 | Byte count of the value |
| 2 | n | Value |

| Item number | Value | When the item is absent |
|---|---|---|
| `01` | **Master pitch.** 2 bytes giving the frequency of A4 in units of 0.1 Hz (4300-4500, low byte first) | 440.0 Hz |
| `02` | **Sequence volume.** 1 byte, 0-127. The volume of all tracks is lowered by as much as this is below 127 (same as `CALL VOLUME` in [`basic-reference.md`](basic-reference.md)) | 127 |
| `03` | **Title.** String | — |
| `04` | **Author name.** String | — |

- **Strings are written with ASCII `20h`-`7Eh` only.** Which characters `80h` and above map to differs by machine and region. There is no end marker; the byte count of the value determines the length
- The same item number must not be written twice. Item numbers not yet defined must not be written either. The reader skips an unknown item number by the byte count of its value
- This ROM skips chunk `80`. `MSAVE` does not write it, so `MLOAD` followed by `MSAVE` loses it

### Limits

The event stream of one track is up to **2048 bytes including the terminating `FF`**. A sequence has 16 tracks, and there are 32 entries in the voice set (16 bytes each for a voice, 36 bytes for a waveform), 3 rhythm voices (16 bytes each), 64 ADPCM voice files (10 bytes each), 31 software envelopes (8 bytes each) and 32 OPM voices (37 bytes each), so a block that does not include OPNA or OPNB is at most 36143 bytes (header 7 + tracks 16×2054 + waveforms 32×36 + rhythm voices 3×16 + voice files 64×10 + envelopes 31×8 + OPM voices 32×37).

OPL3 voices go into the same set, and each is smaller than a waveform (`42` is 29 bytes), so the maximum does not grow. Including those for OPNA and OPNB adds 32 voices each (37 bytes each) and 256 ADPCM-A samples (9 bytes each), for a maximum of 40815 bytes. Meta information (chunk `80`) is not included in these figures.

### OPLLEX, OPL2EX and OPL3 voices

**The record of chunk `01` is the chip's register values packed as they are**, with the same layout for OPLLEX, OPL2EX and OPL3 2OP. The sense of each value also follows the registers. Unused bits and bytes are written as 0. The OPL2EX rhythm voices have the same layout too.

| Offset | Bits | Contents |
|--:|---|---|
| 0 | 3-1 | FB |
| 0 | 0 | C (connection) |
| 1 | 7-0 | Transpose. A signed number of semitones, added to the pitch |
| 2-6 | | OP1 (modulator) |
| 7-11 | | OP2 (carrier) |

Operator (5 bytes).

| Offset | Bits | Contents |
|--:|---|---|
| +0 | 7-6 | KSL |
| +0 | 5-0 | TL |
| +1 | 7-4 | AR |
| +1 | 3-0 | DR |
| +2 | 7-4 | SL |
| +2 | 3-0 | RR |
| +3 | 7 | AM |
| +3 | 6 | VIB |
| +3 | 5 | EGT |
| +3 | 4 | KSR |
| +3 | 3-0 | ML |
| +4 | 2-0 | WS |

- **Fields and bits that a chip does not have are ignored by that chip's reader.** On OPLLEX, C and the carrier TL (the chip's user voice has no place for them); on every chip, the WS bits it does not have (OPLLEX uses only bit0, OPL2EX only bit1-0, OPL3 bit2-0)
- OPLLEX loads this into the chip's user voice. A block can hold only one at a time (see the description of the voice set above)

**The record of chunk `42` (OPL3 4OP, 24 bytes).** The operator layout is the same as for `01`.

| Offset | Bits | Contents |
|--:|---|---|
| 0 | 7-5 | FB2 (FB of the second channel) |
| 0 | 4 | CNT2 (connection of the second channel) |
| 0 | 3-1 | FB1 (FB of the first channel) |
| 0 | 0 | CNT1 (connection of the first channel) |
| 1 | 7-0 | Transpose. A signed number of semitones, added to the pitch |
| 2 | 7-0 | Pseudo-detune. Signed, in units of 1/64 semitone (100/64 cent). Takes effect only when CS is 0 |
| 3 | 0 | CS. 1 plays the pair as 4OP, 0 plays it as two 2OP |
| 4-8 | | OP1 (modulator) |
| 9-13 | | OP2 (carrier) |
| 14-18 | | OP3 (modulator) |
| 19-23 | | OP4 (carrier) |

- OP1 and OP2 are the operators of the first channel of the pair, OP3 and OP4 those of the second channel. FB1 and CNT1 belong to the first channel, FB2 and CNT2 to the second channel
- **When CS is 1**, the pair sounds as 4OP, and the combination of CNT1 and CNT2 determines the algorithm
- **When CS is 0**, the pair sounds as two 2OP. **Key-on and pitch are written to both channels at the same time**, and only the pitch of the second channel is shifted by the pseudo-detune. The amount of shift adds together with transpose and pitch bend
- Bits 7-1 of byte 3 and unused bits are written as 0

### OPM and OPN-family voices

**There is one chunk `40` per index that the tracks of that device name with `85`.** The order of the chunks has no meaning; if the same index of the same device is written twice, the later one remains. A chunk whose index is 32 or above, or whose record is not 32 bytes, causes the whole block to be rejected. The device number is 4, 10 or 11; other numbers must not be written.

**A track that has notes written without a voice being selected, as with OPLLEX, OPL2EX and SCC, takes one index, puts a record in it, and names it with `85` before the first key-on.**

**The record is the chip's register values packed as they are**, with the same layout for OPM and OPNA/OPNB. The sense of each value also follows the registers. A field that exists on only one of the chips is ignored by the other chip's reader. Unused bits and bytes are written as 0.

| Offset | Bits | Contents | |
|--:|---|---|---|
| 0 | 7 | NE (noise) | OPM only |
| 0 | 6 | FX (effect mode) | OPNA, OPNB only |
| 0 | 5-3 | FB | |
| 0 | 2-0 | AL | |
| 1 | 5-4 | AMS | |
| 1 | 2-0 | PMS | |
| 2 | 7-0 | Transpose. A signed number of semitones, added to the pitch | |
| 3 | 7 | Make OP4 sound | |
| 3 | 6 | Make OP3 sound | |
| 3 | 5 | Make OP2 sound | |
| 3 | 4 | Make OP1 sound | |
| 4-10 | | OP1 (M1) | |
| 11-17 | | OP2 (C1) | |
| 18-24 | | OP3 (M2) | |
| 25-31 | | OP4 (C2) | |

Operator (7 bytes).

| Offset | Bits | Contents | |
|--:|---|---|---|
| +0 | 6-0 | TL | |
| +1 | 7-6 | KS | |
| +1 | 4-0 | AR | |
| +2 | 7 | AME | |
| +2 | 4-0 | DR | |
| +3 | 7-6 | DT2 | OPM only |
| +3 | 4-0 | SR | |
| +4 | 7-4 | SL | |
| +4 | 3-0 | RR | |
| +5 | 3-0 | SSG-EG | OPNA, OPNB only |
| +6 | 6-4 | DT | |
| +6 | 3-0 | ML | |

- **Operators are in the order M1, C1, M2, C2 of the algorithm diagram.** This differs from the order of the chip's registers, so the reader reorders them
- **Bits 7-4 of byte 3 are in the same order as the chip's key-on register** (exactly bit7-4 of `28h` on OPNA/OPNB; on OPM they correspond to bit6-3 of `08h`, so shift them right by one bit)
- **NE has meaning only on OPM channel 7, and FX only on OPNA/OPNB channel 2.** Readers for other channels ignore them. The noise frequency is a setting of which the whole chip has only one set, so it is not in the record, and the sequence does not manage it either (see "Common" above). The effect mode pitches are described below
- **The reader for those two channels looks at NE and FX every time a voice is selected, and writes them to the chip whether they are 0 or 1.** Both registers belong to the whole chip, but they take effect only on that channel, so the voice holds them. The destination is bit7 of `0Fh` on OPM (1 for noise), and bit7-6 of `27h` on OPNA/OPNB (`01`, effect mode, if FX is 1; `00`, normal mode, if 0). The other bits of the same register (the noise frequency in `0Fh`, timer control in `27h`) are written without disturbing them. Even if these bits are written with `E0`, they return to the voice's value at the next `85`
- Panning is not in the record. `87` determines it

**In effect mode (a voice with FX set to 1), OP1-OP3 each have their own pitch.** These are called subchannels 1-3, and the pitch of OP4 is taken as the pitch of the parent channel. OP1-OP4 correspond to slots 1-4 in the chip's datasheet, and the registers that hold the pitches are as follows.

| | Slot | Block / F-Number high | F-Number low |
|---|---|---|---|
| Subchannel 1 (OP1) | 1 | `ADh` | `A9h` |
| Subchannel 2 (OP2) | 2 | `AEh` | `AAh` |
| Subchannel 3 (OP3) | 3 | `ACh` | `A8h` |
| Parent (OP4) | 4 | `A6h` | `A2h` (the normal ones for channel 2) |

- Effect mode is when bit7-6 of the chip-wide register `27h` are `01`. The reader writes this when a voice is selected, and returns it to `00` for a voice with FX set to 0 (above)
- For every register, write the high part (the side containing Block) first and the low part after it. The chip latches both when the low part is written

- **`E9` sets a subchannel's pitch as a difference from the parent channel.** The first byte is the subchannel number (1-3; 1 is OP1), and the second and third bytes are the difference. The difference is signed 16-bit (low byte first), and its full range may be used. The unit is 1/64 semitone (100/64 cent), the same as the pseudo-detune
- **At every key-on, the reader sends each subchannel the F-Number for the parent channel's pitch plus that subchannel's difference.** Key-on always happens at the same time as the parent channel — there is no way to key on a subchannel alone
- The difference is running state; its initial value is 0 (all three at the same pitch as the parent), and it returns to 0 at the start of each pass
- **The difference is held regardless of the voice, and used only while a voice with FX set to 1 is selected.** An `E9` that comes while a voice with FX set to 0 is selected also rewrites the difference, and if a voice with FX set to 1 is selected later, it takes effect from that point. As long as it is before the key-on, `85` and `E9` sound the same whichever is written first
- **When the parent channel's pitch changes while it is sounding (pitch bend, portamento), the subchannels follow as well.** Each time the reader writes the parent's pitch, it also writes to each subchannel the pitch with that subchannel's difference added
- On channels other than OPNA/OPNB channel 2, the reader ignores `E9`

## Pitch bend and portamento

### Pitch bend (`D0` `D1`)

The track converts cents into **steps of 1/64 semitone** and holds them, and they are added to the index into the tuning table. 100 cents is exactly 64 steps, and 1200 cents is 768 steps (one octave of the table). Whatever goes beyond the table moves the octave — the table is the same in every octave, so a bend needs only an addition to the index and a fold.

- **Takes effect immediately even on a sounding note.** Writing `D1` alternately with `@W` bends the sound
- `D1` adds, so the total can exceed 1200 cents. **The limit is ±8 octaves** (outside the range of every sound chip), and stopping there serves only to keep the word from wrapping around
- The result of bending to a point outside the range is the same as when a note is outside the range (for the OPL family, the edge of Block 0-7; for divider-based chips, the largest divider value that fits)

### Tie and legato (`45`)

**A property of the next note**, and takes no time itself. It **continues** from the previous note — it issues neither key-off nor key-on, and rewrites only the pitch.

- If the notes before and after are **the same pitch**, it is a tie (the note keeps sounding and nothing changes); if they are **different pitches**, it is legato (the envelope does not restart)
- **On a sound chip that has no key-on, what is suppressed is the envelope restart**
- A rest discards it. What `&` reaches is the next **note**, not a rest
- **The previous note is not keyed off by quantize** ("Quantize" above). When `45` is not immediately after the note — when another event comes in between — the previous note may be keyed off partway through, and in that case there is nothing to continue from, so the next note sounds normally

It uses the same slot as portamento (`D2`) — both only say "the next note continues from what is sounding", and the difference is **whether there is a distance to close**.

### Portamento (`D2`)

**A property of the next note**, and takes no time itself. The length of the next note is used to close the distance, and the pitch arrives just as the note ends.

| Operand | Start point | Sounding |
|---|---|---|
| Cents (`-1200`-`1200`) | The pitch offset from that note by the given amount | **Retriggers** |
| `8000h` | The pitch currently sounding | **Does not retrigger** |
| `0` | — | No portamento. An ordinary note |

`8000h` was chosen as a value the range of cents cannot reach. MML `~` written without a number becomes this. **If nothing is sounding, it sounds as an ordinary note.** A note immediately followed by `D2 8000h` is not keyed off by quantize (the same as `45`).

- It is a separate term from the bend (`D0` `D1`), and the two **add together**. Portamento converges toward the bend value, and the bend remains after the portamento ends
- A rest discards portamento. What `~` reaches is the next **note**, and a rest is not one
- A note without portamento ends any portamento in progress
